paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 4.34 – Alberta Rules of Court – Rule 4 (Part 6)
paragraphs.text: (1) If at any time in an action prior to judgment the interest or liability of a party is transferred or transmitted to another person by assignment, bankruptcy, death or other means, the action is stayed until an order to continue the action by or against the other person has been obtained. (2) If a transfer or transmission of the interest or liability of a party takes place while an application or proceeding in an action is pending, an interested person may, on filing an affidavit verifying the transfer or transmission of the interest or liability and without notice to any other party, request the Court to order that the action continue. (3) An order to continue the action must be served on each of the other parties as soon as it is received by the party requesting the order. (4) If an order to continue an action is not made within a reasonable time after the date on which the action is stayed, the defendant or respondent may apply to the Court to have the action dismissed for delay under rule 4.31.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 4.34:1 Rule 4.34 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 4.34. In Willard Estate v. Compton Petroleum Corp., 2015 ABQB 766, Ward Willard and his company Whispering Winds Stables Inc. filed in 2005 a statement of claim against Compton Petroleum alleging that Compton had breached terms of a surface lease agreement between Compton and the Plaintiffs. The last formal step in the proceedings was taken in 2007. Mr. Willard died in August, 2012. In October, 2013, Compton brought an application for dismissal of the claim (relying on Rules 4.33 and 4.31). Mr. Willard's sister (the self-appointed litigation representative and sole beneficiary of Mr. Willard's estate) applied to continue the action under R. 4.34. Justice Mahoney ruled that the stay referred to in R. 4.34(1) does not, under R. 4.33(1)(b), prevent the application for dismissal under R. 4.33. His Lordship said: 27 The above authorities demonstrate that rules 4.33 and 4.34 must be read together in a manner which achieves the resolution of litigation in a timely fashion, in a manner which is both fair and just. The Master's interpretation of rule 4.34 is at odds with these goals. While rule 4.34(4) expressly preserves the right of a defendant to apply for dismissal under rule 4.31, I do not find that its failure to mention rule 4.33 translates into a legislative intent to remove the ability of a defendant to apply for relief under rule 4.33. To find otherwise removes one of the key ways in which a litigant can dispose of a stale claim in a timely and cost effective manner. 28 Rule 4.34(4) provides that if an order to continue a stayed action is not made within a reasonable amount of time, a defendant may apply to have the action dismissed for delay under rule 4.31. Compton argues that the Master interpreted the word “may” in this subrule to mean “shall”, thus creating a situation whereby the sole recourse available to a defendant where an action has been stayed by the Rules, yet over three years of inactivity have passed, is a delay of action application under 4.31. 29 Given the wording of both rules 4.33 and 4.34, as read against the foundational principles, this cannot be what the Legislature envisaged. 30 Although similar in outcome, rules 4.33 and 4.31 remain distinct. Rule 4.33 is simply unavailable to an applicant until three years have passed without any significant advancement in the action. After this period of time it becomes a very powerful tool. Rule 4.31 deals with situations where the delay faced is presumably short of the three year delay dealt with in 4.33: Le at para 43. Ostensibly, in exchange for having an action dismissed despite a shorter period of inactivity, the applicant must demonstrate prejudice. It functions, amongst other things, as a case management tool. 31 The two rules are designed to work together and to complement other rules in order to achieve the timely and cost effective resolution of court actions. There is nothing in the language of subrule 4.34(4)—express or implied—which indicates a legislative intent to remove the ability of a defendant to benefit under the drop dead rule. Subrule (4) simply states that if a stay imposed under subrule (1) is in place, and no order to continue the action is made within a reasonable time, a defendant may apply for relief under rule 4.31 notwithstanding the stay. There is nothing in this language suggesting that additional avenues open to a defendant in cases of delay become unavailable. Rules 4.33 and 4.34 can operate together and the permissive language used in rule 4.34(4) does not displace the availability of alternate remedies under 4.33. 32 An ordinary and contextual reading of subrule (4), given the object of the Rules, does not suggest that a defendant's exclusive remedy lies under rule 4.31. The permissive language used in rule 4.34(4) strongly intimates that it should not be read in a fashion which takes away or displaces rights provided for under other rules. 33 Support for this interpretation is found in the wording of rule 4.33(1)(b). It provides that if more than three years go by without a significant advance in an action, the court, on application, must dismiss the action unless it “has been stayed or adjourned by order, an order has extended the time for advancing the action, or the delay is provided for in a litigation plan”. … 38 As such, reading rules 4.33 and 4.34 together leads to the conclusion that a stay imposed under 4.34(1) does not qualify as the type of stay included in the exemptions listed in 4.33(1)(b). When the two rules are read together, I conclude that the Master erred in finding rule 4.33 inapplicable and in reading rule 4.34(4) as restricting the remedies available to Compton to a rule 4.31 application. Justice Bast in Harrington v. Stackard, 2016 ABQB 357, 2016 CarswellAlta 1221 agreed with Justice Mahoney's decision in Willard Estate v. Compton Petroleum Corp., 2015 ABQB 766. In OmniArch Capital Corporation v. Bishop, 2020 ABQB 102, 2020 CarswellAlta 287, Madam Justice Dilts said: [17] Under Rule 4.34, this action was automatically stayed when OmniArch assigned its interest in this litigation to Durum Opportunities LP. There are only two permissible next steps where an action has been stayed: either the plaintiff brings an application to continue the action or, where the plaintiff has not done so within a reasonable time after the date on which the action was stayed, the defendant brings an application under Rule 4.34(4) to have the action dismissed for delay under Rule 4.31. [18] Applications for continuation invite an inquiry into the reason for the assignment to prevent intermeddling in litigation for collateral reasons. The court is to determine whether there are valid reasons for the assignment or whether there are any legal or policy reasons against continuing the action. An assignment is considered valid if the assignee has a genuine commercial interest in taking the assignment and enforcing the litigation or, in the case of an action in tort, if the assignee possesses a sufficient pre-existing interest in the cause of action: Fredrickson v Insurance Corp. of British Columbia (1986) 1986 CanLII 1066 (BC CA), 3 BCLR (2d) 145 (CA), aff'd 1988 CanLII 38 (SCC), [1988] 1 SCR 1089 (SCC). … [21] As already noted, Rule 4.34(4) says that “[i]f an order to continue an action is not made within a reasonable time after the date on which the action is stayed, the defendant or respondent may apply to the Court to have the action dismissed for delay under rule 4.31.” Even where there has been an unreasonable period of time between the assignment and the bringing of an application to continue the action, Rule 4.34(4) does not itself authorize the court to dismiss an action for delay. Instead, it creates a pathway to Rule 4.31. … [23] There was some discussion whether Rule 4.34 authorizes me to continue the action against some but not all parties, in essence to dismiss the action against Crowe MacKay by allowing the action to continue only against the Defaulting Defendants. Rule 4.34 authorizes the continuation of “the action”. Unlike other Rules, including Rule 4.31, Rule 4.34 does not permit relief to extend to only some of the Defendants nor, as I have already said, does it create the authority to dismiss a claim against a defendant distinct from the considerations in Rule 4.31. Therefore, while Crowe MacKay says the Plaintiffs did not bring this continuation application within a reasonable time of the assignment, even had it been successful in that regard, it simply points the parties to the considerations under Rule 4.31. [24] My authority under Rule 4.34 is to continue the action as a whole. Whether Crowe MacKay is entitled to have the action against it dismissed for delay is properly considered under Rule 4.31. I therefore grant the Plaintiffs' application to continue the action and to file the Amended Statement of Claim substituting Durum Opportunities GP Inc. and Durum Opportunities LP as Plaintiffs. 1. Family law actions and Bankruptcy In Jesson v. Jesson, 2021 ABQB 93, 2021 CarswellAlta 257, Ms. Jesson commenced actions against Mr. Jesson for spousal and child support, and a division of matrimonial property. Mr. Jesson had filed for bankruptcy, and a stay of Ms. Jesson's matrimonial property action had been entered pursuant to the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act (Canada). Ms. Jesson applied for an order lifting the stay. Justice Yungwirth granted an order under Rule 4.34 permitting the previously stayed actions to continue. Her Ladyship said: [14] The intersection of family law and bankruptcy is an area where much reform is needed. The above summary highlights the difficulties that arise when a bankruptcy stalls the divorce and matrimonial property proceedings and interferes with the disclosure process that would allow property and support issues to be determined. … [21] As the stay provisions in s. 69.3 of the BIA apply only to claims provable in bankruptcy, they do not apply to the claims of Ms. Jesson in her combined divorce and matrimonial property proceeding. [22] Ms. Jesson's child support claims are also not “provable” in the bankruptcy because the existing support order was not made before the date of the bankruptcy. [23] A support claim may be prosecuted in personam against the bankrupt without leave of the bankruptcy court while the debtor spouse is an undischarged bankrupt and afterward. Saberi v Saberi, 1979 CanLII 3679 (Ont CA), referenced by the ABQB in Cousin v Cousin, 2020 ABQB 636. [24] Any ongoing child support payable pursuant to an order obtained after the date of the bankruptcy should be factored into Mr. Jesson's monthly expenses when the Trustee is calculating the bankrupt's monthly surplus. However, the enforcement of arrears of child support against the assets of the bankrupt that have vested in the Trustee, is prohibited by ss. 69.41(2) of the BIA. Enforcement of such arrears is limited to the BIA exempt assets of the bankrupt and the portion of the bankrupt's income in excess of any payments to the estate. [25] Ms. Jesson concedes that rule 4.34 of the Rules operates to stay her action as a result of the vesting of Mr. Jesson's property interests in the Trustee in bankruptcy. … [26] Pursuant to rule 12.35 of the Rules, rule 4.34 does not operate to stay a proceeding under the Divorce Act, RSC 1985, c-3. So, rule 4.34 can apply only to the matrimonial property proceeding in this case. [27] Rule 4.34 itself sets out the procedure to be followed by someone in the position of Ms. Jesson, to obtain an order that her action continue. It can be done without notice to any other party. The Trustee in bankruptcy essentially “inherits” the divorce and matrimonial property actions as they stand. [28] There does not appear to be any “test” to apply when considering if an application made pursuant to rule 4.34(2) should be granted. Though there may be cases where it would not be appropriate to order that the action continue, this is not one of them. A spouse should not be able to use the bankruptcy system to stall their obligation to disclose and to prevent a fulsome consideration and determination of matrimonial property entitlements, either under the former Matrimonial Property Act, RSA 2000, Chapter M-8 (MPA), or the Family Property Act, RSA 2000, Chapter F-4.7 (FPA). [29] Families and children suffer when their family property and divorce issues remain unresolved. If there is no determination of Ms. Jesson's property interests (which would consider any MPA or FPA exemption claims by either party), there is a risk that those interests might be unfairly divided among Mr. Jesson's creditors in the bankruptcy. [30] Ms. Jesson is entitled to proceed with her divorce and matrimonial property action so that she can verify Mr. Jesson's income, assets and liabilities for the purpose of determining and enforcing her support and property claims. The Trustee has the right to and should be involved (pursuant to s. 81 of the BIA) so that the division of matrimonial property can be finalized and the Trustee can determine the property available for the creditors of Mr. Jesson (e.g. a matrimonial property exemption that does not have to be shared with Ms. Jesson). Even without the Trustee's involvement, Ms. Jesson is entitled to enforce her child support arrears against Mr. Jesson's BIA exempt assets. As the welfare of the children is involved, that alone is sufficient reason to order that the actions continue. [31] I hereby order that the divorce and matrimonial property actions will continue. 2. In a multi-party action, is the whole action stayed? In Matthews v. Lawrence, 2021 ABQB 776, 2021 CarswellAlta 2342, additional reasons 2022 ABQB 288, there were 22 plaintiffs and 14 defendants. One of the plaintiffs and one of the defendants died. The question arose whether those deaths resulted in the entirety of the action being stayed by operation of R. 4.34(1). Justice Devlin concluded that the stay under R. 4.34(1) only operated against the parties whose interests were transferred by reason of their deaths. His Lordship said: [33] The question arising in this case is whether the rule stays the entirety of the action or only as against the party whose interests were transferred, in this case by death. In my respectful view, the rule only stays the action against those parties whose interests have transferred by operation of one of the mechanisms enumerated in the rule. [34] It makes little intuitive sense that the death of one of 22 Plaintiffs, and one of 15 Defendants, would stall an entire proceeding. Indeed, the individual Defendant died well before the remaining Defendants served their Affidavit of Records, and yet their solicitors appear never to have turned their minds to this. [35] While this facet of Rule 4.34 has not directly been considered by a Court in Alberta, the effect of virtually identical wording in Ontario's R 11.01 has been. In Green Bay Packaging Inc v Meco Group Inc, [1999] OJ No 3120 (Sup Ct J) at para 22, Nordheimer J (as he then was) reached the following conclusion: I do not accept that a fair or reasonable reading of rule 11 leads to the conclusion that the whole proceeding is stayed. I believe that rule 11 fairly read is referring to the proceeding as regards the party whose interest or liability is concerned. The reference in the rule to obtaining an order to continue the proceeding against the person reinforces my view that this is the proper interpretation to give to the rule. It makes no sense to me that where there are multiple parties and one of those parties becomes bankrupt the entire proceeding would be stayed. Rather, in such a situation, I would view the reasonable result to be that the proceeding estate against banker party but can proceeding as the others. The opposing party would then, presumably, either obtain an order to permit the action to proceed against banker party with simple except that the action is stated and just deal with the parties remaining. [36] I find this reasoning compelling. In multiparty actions of this nature, there is no good or practical reason why the litigation cannot proceed apace despite the death of one individual, whose involvement may well be peripheral. For instance, if such a party passed away on the eve of a major motion being argued, or other step being taken, it would be both unnecessary and slightly absurd to hold that the entire process must automatically be put on hold, potentially resulting in significant costs and time being wasted. [37] Contrary to what the Defendants argue, the fact that Justice Nordheimer's analysis took place in the context of bankruptcy does not alter the analysis. Reading Rule 4.34 in the same manner is more consistent with common sense and the foundational rules. [38] Moreover, section 10 of the Interpretation Act requires me to construe legislation “as being remedial” and by giving it a “fair, large and liberal construction and interpretation that best ensures the attainment of its objectives”. The cardinal rules of statutory interpretation, which apply to the Rules, also compel me to “read the words of an Act in their entire context and in their grammatical and ordinary sense harmoniously with the scheme of the Act, the object of the Act and the intention of Parliament”: Rizzo & Rizzo Shoes Ltd (Re), [1988] 2 SCR 27 at para 21. In this case, that underlying objective of Rule 4.34 the timely and efficient advancement of litigation. That objective is better served by holding that litigation is only stayed against parties whose interests have been transferred, irrespective of the mechanism underlying that transfer.

[37] Contrary to what the Defendants argue, the fact that Justice Nordheimer's analysis took place in the context of bankruptcy does not alter the analysis.
Reading Rule 4.34 in the same manner is more consistent with common sense and the foundational rules.

[38] Moreover, section 10 of the Interpretation Act requires me to construe legislation “as being remedial” and by giving it a “fair, large and liberal construction and interpretation that best ensures the attainment of its objectives”.

The cardinal rules of statutory interpretation, which apply to the Rules, also compel me to “read the words of an Act in their entire context and in their grammatical and ordinary sense harmoniously with the scheme of the Act, the object of the Act and the intention of Parliament”: Rizzo & Rizzo Shoes Ltd (Re), [1988] 2 SCR 27 at para 21.
In this case, that underlying objective of Rule 4.34 the timely and efficient advancement of litigation.
That objective is better served by holding that litigation is only stayed against parties whose interests have been transferred, irrespective of the mechanism underlying that transfer.

paragraphs.text: (1) Before a date is set for trial, a plaintiff may discontinue all or any part of an action against one or more defendants. (2) After a trial date has been set but before a trial starts, a plaintiff may discontinue all or part of an action against one or more defendants only (a) with the written agreement of every party, or (b) with the Court's permission. (3) After the trial starts, a plaintiff may discontinue all or part of an action only with the Court's permission. (4) A discontinuance under this rule must be in Form 23 and must be filed and served on each of the other parties and, after the plaintiff serves notice of discontinuance, the defendant is entitled to a costs award against the plaintiff for having defended against the discontinued claim. (5) The discontinuance of the action may not be raised as a defence to any subsequent action for the same or substantially the same claim.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 4.36:1 Rule 4.36 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 4.36. 1. Old Rule and New Rule In Newel Post Developments Ltd. v. 1402801 Alberta Ltd., 2012 ABQB 422, 2012 CarswellAlta 1149, 543 A.R. 79, Chief Justice Wittmann said, at paragraph 36: “There is no material difference between the new ARC [Alberta Rule of Court] and old ARC governing the obligation of a party to obtain leave of the Court to discontinue an action or claim.” 2. Withdrawing an Originating Application In Shergill v. Skene, 2011 ABQB 334, 2011 CarswellAlta 877, 26 C.P.C. (7th) 406 (Master), Master Prowse said, at paragraphs 4-9, and 16: 4 The rules of court do not directly address the withdrawal of an originating application. 5 Rule 1.7(2) says that the rules may be applied by analogy to any matter arising that is not dealt with in the rules. 6 Counsel for the Skenes says that an analogy should be made to the situation which occurs when a plaintiff discontinues an action, commenced by statement of claim, after it has been set down for trial. In that case, Rule 4.36(2)(b) indicates that the action may only be discontinued with the court's permission. I agree that this withdrawal is an analogous situation in that Shergill's originating application was on the verge of being heard when it was withdrawn. Consequently, Shergill needs the court's permission for that withdrawal. What is the purpose of requiring the court's permission for a discontinuance/withdrawal? 7 The court requires control over discontinuances to prevent plaintiffs, who have caused defendants to expend time and resources in defending an action, from unilaterally discontinuing an action, leaving the plaintiffs free (subject to limitations issues) to re-litigate the same issues at a time of their choosing in the future. Options available to the Court 8 Does the court's jurisdiction to grant or withhold permission for a discontinuance or withdrawal include the jurisdiction to impose terms on the discontinuance or withdrawal? 9 According to the Civil Procedure Encyclopedia “where leave is needed to discontinue, the court can impose terms”. Case law is then cited in support of the proposition that one of the terms which can be imposed is that the plaintiff/applicant cannot sue again. … 16 The Alberta rule on discontinuing with leave, Rule 4.36(2)(b), does not expressly list a bar on subsequent proceedings as something which can be imposed, in contrast to the rules in Ontario and Nova Scotia. However, given that the abuse of possible re-litigation is what Rule 4.36(2)(b) appears designed to control, I am of the view that it is implicit that the court may impose such a term pursuant to Rule 4.36(2)(b). 3. Setting Aside Discontinuance Master Funduk continued: In Kennedy v. Gunnar-Nesbitt Aviation Ltd., [1973] 5 W.W.R. 41 (Alta. S.C.T.D.), the plaintiff applied for an order to “withdraw and cancel” a discontinuance. Cullen, J., concludes the court has jurisdiction to allow the withdrawal of a dicontinuance [sic]which had been properly filed. It is clear he considered it a matter of discretion, to be exercised on proper grounds. He found, on the facts before him, that it would not be appropriate to allow the discontinuance to be withdrawn. That decision was appealed but abandoned: see Kennedy v. Saddy, [1975] 4 W.W.R. 651 (Alta. C.A.), at p. 654: In Allard v. Manaham, [1975] 3 W.W.R. 371 (B.C. C.A.), the plaintiff, at trial, obtained leave to discontinue the action against two defendants. Leave was granted. The plaintiff later applied to set aside the order granting leave to discontinue. A limitation period had accrued. In reversing the chambers judge, who had granted the application to set aside the leave to discontinue, Robertson, J.A., states at pp. 375-376: What principles, if any, govern the exercise of that discretion? Mr. Buchanan, for the respondent, submitted that the discretion was unfettered so long as it was exercised judicially. Mr. Giles, for the appellant, submitted that in this case the discretion should be exercised only if very special circumstances exist, and he likened the matter to one where an application is made to renew a writ that has not been served within time. While the two cases are not necessarily on all fours, I do think that the principle to which I shall next refer should be applied here. In Cropp v. Moreton, [1975] 1 W.W.R. 637 (B.C. C.A.), I said this in a judgment with which Maclean, J.A., agreed (Seaton, J.A., dissenting) (p. 644): So far as granting an extension of time for an application under R. 1 of 0.8 after the expiry of the writ and after a claim has become statute barred is concerned, in Kelly v. Schuitema (1964), 48 W.W.R. (N.S.) 491 … Bird, J.A., with whom Norris, J.A., and Lord, J.A., agreed, said in this court at p. 493: I take the effect of the English cases to be that the discretionary power conferred by M.R. 967 to renew a writ after the time for service fixed by M.R. 45 has expired will not be exercised when the effect of the renewal will be to deprive the defendant of a limitation which has accrued, unless very special circumstances are shown to justify the exercise of that discretion. The requirement that there must be ‘very special circumstances’ in such a case as this was applied again by this court in Burns & Dutton Concrete & Construction Co. v. Dominion Insur. Corpn. (1966), 55 W.W.R. (N.S.) 619 … The reason for the requirement is, of course, that a statute of limitation is not a mere technical defence—see Beattie v. Dorosz, [1932] 2 W.W.R. 289 (Sask. C.A.), and Miller v. C.P.R., [1933] 1 W.W.R. 233 (Alta. C.A.), and a right thereunder once accrued is not lightly to be taken away. Robertson, J.A., then goes on to consider whether there were “very special circumstances” and whether there was a proper exercise of discretion by the chambers judge. The point of Allard is that where a limitation period has accrued, a discontinuance can be withdrawn only if there are “very special circumstances”. The test appears to be equivalent to that enunciated in Baskarsky v. Quinlan, [1972] 1 W.W.R. 303 (S.C.C.). In Kennedy Cullen, J., discusses the matter in relation to a “properly filed” discontinuance. By that I take it to mean a case where the plaintiff intended to discontinue and the exercise of the discontinuance (if it was filed by the defendant) was not improper. One can readily visualise situations where the discontinuance is not proper, not from a procedural point of view, but a substantive point of view. For example, the plaintiff has a number of unrelated separate actions against the same defendant. The plaintiff intends to discontinue one of the actions, but in error files the discontinuance in the wrong action. That is a case where the mind does not accompany the hand. Another example might be where the plaintiff delivers a discontinuance to the defendant subject to conditions and the defendant, in breach of the conditions, files the discontinuance. In such a case the defendant should not be allowed to bootstrap himself up by his wrongdoing. A further example might be where the defendant manages to extract a discontinuance from the plaintiff by a misrepresentation or fraud of another nature, or by duress, undue influence or the like. However, where the discontinuance was proper in the sense that the plaintiff did intend to discontinue and there was no substantive impropriety on the part of the defendant, the special circumstances would be rare. Allowing a discontinuance to be withdrawn after a limitation period has accrued is in substance equivalent to allowing an amendment to a statement of claim after the limitation period has accrued. The discontinuance means there is no longer an action against the defendant against whom the action was discontinued. The withdrawal of a discontinuance has the effect of making the defendant a party as of the date the action had been commenced, just as an amendment which adds a defendant “relates back” that defendant to the date the action was commenced. In my view, the appropriate test for the withdrawal of a discontinuance is that suggested in Allard, without the emphasizer. Eisenkrein v. Eisenkrein (1984), 53 A.R. 199 at 206-207 (Master). In Yancey v. Neis (1999), 73 Alta. L.R. (3d) 239 (C.A.), Madam Justice Russell held that the analytical approach is to be applied in applications to set aside a discontinuance. For an explanation of the analytical approach, see the annotation “Limitations” under R. 3.75. In Her Ladyship's decision, she agreed with Master Funduk in Eisenkrein v. Eisenkrein (1984), 53 A.R. 199 (Master). At pp. 247-48, Russell J.A. said: Such an approach accords with the decision of Master Funduk in Eisenkrein v. Eisenkrein (1984), 53 A.R. 199 (Alta. Master), where he stated at para. 43, that: allowing a discontinuance after a limitation period has accrued is in substance equivalent to allowing an amendment to a statement of claim. He therefore adopted the test for the withdrawal of a discontinuance equivalent to that enunciated in Basarsky v. Quinlan, supra, stating that “where a limitation period has accrued, a discontinuance can be withdrawn only if there are ‘very special circumstances’” such as where a plaintiff discontinued the wrong action, or where the defendant breached conditions upon which the discontinuance was given. Special circumstances have also been defined to include cases of “inadvertence, mistake or mispprehension of relevant procedural matter”… Such circumstances suggest oversight rather than the sort or substantive mistakes of law in this case. Hence, I agree with Master Funduk that special circumstances in the nature of a slip must be established before a discontinuance may be withdrawn. Therefore, special circumstances must include an absence of actual prejudice to the defendant: Basarsky v. Quinlan, as well as a consideration of the circumstances giving rise to the discontinuance. . . . . . … a finding of no actual prejudice is not determinative. It is only one factor to be considered in establishing whether there are special circumstances. In addition to finding the discontinuance resulted from a slip or oversight, the determination of whether special circumstances exist in an application to withdraw a discontinuance must include consideration of whether the plaintiff can show that the defendant has not been prejudiced because timely notice can be inferred from her prior connection to the pleadings. Finally, Her Ladyship noted that “misapprehension of the law is not a special circumstance” (p. 250). 4. Purpose of the Rule In Coyle v. Coyle Estate, 2005 ABQB 436, 2005 CarswellAlta 842, 383 A.R. 135, 56 Alta. L.R. (4th) 373, Greckol J. said, at p. 379: The purpose of Rule 225(1) appears to be to ensure that the defendant in such a case is protected in respect of taxable costs that may have been incurred in defending the action. … Rule 225(3) states that, except as otherwise provided in Rule 225, a plaintiff may not withdraw any claim or discontinue an action without leave of the court. However, the court may, before, at or after the hearing or trial, on such terms as to costs or otherwise as may seem just, order the action to be discontinued or any claim struck out. Leave is required under this Rule in recognition that, once proceedings have reached an advanced stage, the plaintiff is no longer dominus litus, and the defendant may have an interest in the case proceeding: British Columbia (Minister of Forests) v. Okanagan Indian Band 2005 CarswellBC 743, 2005 BCSC 492 (B.C. S.C.); see also Berry v. Cypost Corp. 2004 CarswellBC 302, 2004 BCSC 206 (B.C. S.C.); Schlund v. Foster (1908), 11 O.W.R. 175 (Ont. H.C.). … In De Shazo v. Nations Energy Co., 2006 ABCA 400, 2006 CarswellAlta 1716, 401 A.R. 142, 68 Alta. L.R. (4th) 57, the Court held that the right to file a discontinuance of action could not be used to effect an abuse of the court's process. In that case, the defendants gave two weeks notice of their application for summary dismissal of the plaintiff's claim (far in excess of the two days notice required). The plaintiff used the additional time to file a discontinuance of action. The Court of Appeal ordered that the discontinuance of action be set aside because it was an abuse of the court's process. At paragraphs 7-15, the Court said: Discontinuances are dealt with in R. 225 …. As can be seen, the Rule is absolute in its wording and does not mention any limitations on the plaintiff's right to discontinue. The appellant relies on Coyle v. Coyle Estate 2005 ABQB 436, 18 C.P.C. (6th) 630, [2006] 4 W.W.R. 268. The Coyles separated in 1997 and Mrs. Coyle commenced a matrimonial property action in 1998. Mr. Coyle failed to defend and was noted in default in 1998. Nothing further was done to advance the action before Mr. Coyle died in March of 2002. Mrs. Coyle filed a discontinuance of the matrimonial property action in September of 2004. Because the limitation period had expired, the effect of the discontinuance was that the Coyle Estate could no longer seek a division of the matrimonial property. The court concluded that the right to discontinue was unconditional and declined to set aside the discontinuance. The decision in Coyle did not consider abuse of process. The defendant in that case had allowed himself to be noted in default, thereby giving up his right to contest the claim or to receive notice of any steps in the proceedings. The discontinuance was not filed for any collateral purpose, such as an attempt to export the litigation, block any legitimate pending procedural step by the defendant, or to otherwise prevent the court from exercising its jurisdiction. Since Mr. Coyle had neither commenced his own action within the limitation period, or counter-claimed within the action commenced by Mrs. Coyle, and given the lengthy delay, there was arguably no abuse of process. The circumstances in the present appeal are clearly distinguishable. The appellant also relies on Fox v. Star Newspaper Company, [1898] 1 Q.B. 636; affirmed, [1900] A.C. 19, where the plaintiff attempted to discontinue without leave after the trial had commenced. The Court held at 639: The principle of the rule is plain. It is that after the proceedings have reached a certain stage the plaintiff, who has brought his adversary into court, shall not be able to escape by a side door and avoid the contest. He is then to be no longer dominus litis, and it is for the judge to say whether the action shall be discontinued or not and upon what terms. The decision in Fox is sound, but it does not follow that prior to the commencement of trial, the plaintiff can discontinue regardless of the effect that may have on the rights of the defendants. The appellant argues that R. 225 is a complete code on the subject of discontinuances: McGee v. Canada Coachlines Ltd., [1946] O.W.N. 73 (M); Lye v. McConnell (1905), 5 O.W.R. 326 at para. 7. Whether a rule can be described as a “complete code” or not, no rule should be read to countenance abuses of process. It is not necessary for each rule to open with the declaration “except in the case of an abuse of process”. There is contrary authority holding that the court does have a residual discretion to set aside a discontinuance and therefore, the court can regard a discontinuance as being ineffective in the right circumstances: Kennedy v. Gunnar-Nesbitt Aviation Ltd., [1973] 5 W.W.R. 41, 38 D.L.R. (3rd) 288 (Alta S.C.); Angelopoulos v. Angelopoulos (1986), 9 C.P.C. (2d) 285 (Ont. H.C.J.). Notwithstanding the absolute wording of the Rule, we are satisfied that the court possesses an inherent jurisdiction to control its process: I. H. Jacobs “The Inherent Jurisdiction of the Court,” (1970), 23 Current Legal Problems 23 at 25, cited with approval in MacMillan Bloedel Ltd. v. Simpson, [1995] 4 S.C.R. 725 and Toronto (City) v. Canadian Union of Public Employees (C.U.P.E.), Local 79 2003 SCC 63, [2003] 3 S.C.R. 77 at paras. 35 and 37. The Rules of Court are designed to enable the fair, economical and efficient adjudication of a civil claim. Where the Rules are used in an obstructive, abusive or unfair manner, the court has the inherent jurisdiction to intervene, especially where the ability of the court to adjudicate on the merits is involved. While the appellant might have a wide ranging right to discontinue the action, the defendants have an equal right to bring an application for summary dismissal. Just as there are no conditions listed in R. 225 on the right to discontinue, there are no conditions listed in R. 159(2) on the right to seek summary dismissal. Rule 225(1) merely provides that the ability of a plaintiff to discontinue an action before trial is not conditional on the approval of a judge: compare R. 225(3). Rule 225 is not an absolute rule in isolation from other rules providing for adjudications by the Court of Queen's Bench, and does not provide that a discontinued action shall immediately be treated as if it never existed. The appellant notes that no application was brought to set aside the discontinuance. While such a formal application might have been desirable, there can be no suggestion that the appellant was taken by surprise, or that any prejudice resulted from the procedure followed. It could equally be argued that the appellant took no steps to set aside the applications for summary dismissal. Under the Rules, the defendants could have brought their summary judgment applications on two days notice. Instead, they gave approximately two weeks notice to provide the appellant with a reasonable opportunity to respond. The appellant used this period of time to file a discontinuance of action and thereby attempted to deprive the defendants of their right to seek summary dismissal. This was prejudicial to the defendants and abusive of the processes of the court. The chambers judge was correct to proceed in the face of the discontinuance. In Simbajon v. Leduc, 2015 ABCA 321, Justice O'Ferrall, in dismissing an application to extend the time to file an appeal, said at paragraph 19: “The law with respect to when a statement of claim may or may not be discontinued has been settled by the decision of this court in De Shazo. It may be discontinued in accordance with the Rules so long as to do so would not constitute an abuse of process or be unfair.” In Simbajon v. Leduc, 2015 ABCA 321, the applicant had commenced a matrimonial property action by Statement of Claim. She sought to discontinue that action on the eve of an agreed-upon, binding judicial dispute resolution. As Justice O'Ferrall said at paragraph 21: 21 It is also important to point out that although the matter had not been set for trial, as contemplated by Rule 4.36(1), the matter had been set for an agreed-upon binding judicial dispute resolution, something clearly analogous to a trial. The JDR was to have been heard on June 16, 2015, but instead of participating in the JDR, the applicant indicated her intention to discontinue her claim. The court below, therefore, was called upon to adjudicate upon the respondent's application to prevent discontinuance on the basis that it was either an abuse of process or an attempt to unfairly avoid adjudication of his matrimonial property claim. In those circumstances, the Court has a residual discretion to control its processes, including setting aside a discontinuance or preventing one from being filed if it constituted an abuse of process or was otherwise manifestly unfair. In this case, the chambers judge quite properly found the prospect of a discontinuance to be both. I agree. 5. Costs In Dool Estate, Re, 2007 ABQB 12, 2007 CarswellAlta 19, 413 A.R. 222, 71 Alta. L.R. (4th) 146, Clark J. made the following comments about costs when actions are discontinued (at pp. 231-232): 36 Discontinuances are often heard by way of an application to the Court for adjudication with respect to costs, pursuant to Rule 225(3) of the Alberta Rules of Court, or by consent of all parties, pursuant to Rule 225(5). Therefore, it is not uncommon for such discontinuances to be made subject to adjudication with respect to costs. In such circumstances, the Court maintains its discretion and may make any costs order that it deems fair and equitable when considering all of the circumstances. Only when a party discontinues its action unilaterally with neither application to the Court nor agreement is the Court's discretion expressly restricted, pursuant to Rule 225(1). 37 It is sometimes said that the general rule in cases of discontinuance is that the plaintiff will ordinarily have to pay the costs of the opposing party. However, as discussed further below, the rules of general litigation are not always applied in estate matters. Secondly, the Alberta Court of Appeal stated in Canadian Mortgage Investment Co. v. Teel (No. 2), [1923] 1 D.L.R. 576 (Alta. S.C.A.D.) that the policy reason for this general rule is that a discontinuance normally implies that the plaintiff has concluded he or she cannot win, or that his or her claim is defective or illegitimate. It follows that this general rule does not apply in cases where the plaintiff is able to establish that the discontinuance is based on other extenuating circumstances and that the claim is reasonable. 38 For instance, it was held in Brown v. Leech (1998), 76 A.C.W.S. (3d) 1076 (Ont. Gen. Div.) that in cases where a plaintiff is able to show that it was reasonable to bring a claim against the defendant, and the plaintiff has then discontinued as soon as reasonably possible, resulting in the avoidance of expensive litigation, the plaintiff may be permitted to discontinue without costs. By contrast, in Yedlinski v. Kasha (1988), 63 Alta. L.R. (2d) 139 (Q.B.), Master Funduk held that “on the scant facts” before him and given the plaintiff's failure to provide any legitimate explanation as to why he wished to discontinue, it was improper to depart from the general rule that the plaintiff pay costs. 39 In this case, there are numerous compelling and special circumstances that justify a discontinuance without costs. The Applicants are not applying to discontinue because they have realized they have a faulty claim or cannot win. The Applicants respectfully assert that they have a strong claim and, absent the very serious health and financial issues with which both are struggling, coupled with the stonewalling caused by the Respondent, they would continue to pursue that claim. They would seek enforcement of the October 9, 2002 Order for a full and complete accounting and disclosure, and, should it appear to be reasonable and necessary based on the information so obtained, would proceed to trial. 40 There is recent authority for the proposition that health issues constitute special circumstances in which the plaintiff will be permitted to discontinue without costs. In Donlevy v. Donlevy (1999), 191 Sask.R. 152 (Q.B.), the Court permitted the plaintiff to do so after she adduced evidence that the stress of the contentious litigation was impeding her ability to cope with depression and that she was unemployed and could not afford to continue, despite a legitimate claim. The Court expressly pointed out that the defendant could not be regarded as a “successful litigant” who was entitled to costs pursuant to the general rule that costs follow the event, saying at para. 10 that “The issue was not adjudicated in his favour. The litigation process was stopped short of adjudication by the petitioner's illness.” The Court concluded its reasons by stating as follows: I cannot get beyond [respondent] counsel's invitation to infer that the petitioner discontinued her claim because she thought it lacked merit. She swears she discontinued because of her mental health. She presented medical evidence … I am asked to ignore that evidence and speculate that she discontinued her claim for the reason suggested by counsel, raised by his inference alone and unsupported by evidence. Her claim has not been adjudged unmeritorious. It has only been denounced as such by counsel. That is not sufficient for me to exercise my discretion in favour of his client. There will be no order for costs. 41 In my view, this case is analogous to Donlevy in that the discontinuance is sought, not because the Applicants have concluded that their claim is unmeritorious, but rather due to extenuating circumstances of serious illness and financial difficulties. 6. Death of Plaintiff Is Not Enough to Avoid Costs Per Master Funduk: This is an application by the plaintiff for an order allowing her to discontinue the action without costs … The only fact counsel for the plaintiff relies on for saying that the plaintiff should not have to pay costs is that she has died. Depending on one's philosophy about the origins of mankind, it might be suggested that here there was an unexpected intervention by a divine third party over whom neither side has any control. I would not extend the reach of Can. Mtge. and Park to encompass that kind of intervention, which is a certainty for all of us. The intervention in Can. Mtge. and Park had a direct effect on the cause of action. In one case it effectively gave the cause of action in a roundabout way and in the other it effectively extinguished it. The plaintiff's death does not affect the cause of action in any legal sense. She claims a breach of contract by the Kashas and claims in debt for $15,000 and interest. That cause of action, if there is one, survives the plaintiff's death. All we have here is a case where the plaintiff's representative has decided not to pursue the action, for whatever reason. I could understand the application if the relief that was being sought in the action was something personal to the plaintiff only, that is, going more to her person that to her pocketbook. That is not the case here. The plaintiff seeks a money judgment against the Kashas which claim survives her death and which, if successfully prosecuted by the plaintiff's representative, would result in a money judgment against the Kashas, which would be an asset of the estate. The plaintiff has not satisfied me that a proper exercise of discretion is to allow her to discontinue without costs. To the contrary, I consider it would be an improper exercise of discretion to allow a discontinuance without costs on the scant facts before me. Yedlinski v. Kasha (1988), 63 Alta. L.R. (2d) 139 at 140 and 142-43 (Master). 7. Discontinuance of Action Gone to Judgment One cannot discontinue after an action in which judgment has been taken and an order nisi order for sale is a judgment. Of great interest to the question of whether or not an order nisi order for sale is a judgment is the case of Mfrs. Life Ins. Co. v. Mehra, [1982] A.W.L.D. 1132 … In that case the master reviewed some of the authorities involving order nisi order for sale and came to the conclusion that, despite its label, it is in fact a judgment. This proposition of course was supported by the case of Webmore Financial Services Ltd. v. James M. Drummond Holdings Ltd. (1981), 33 A.R. 493 (Q.B.). I agree with the proposition as stated by Funduk, Master in the Mfr. Life case, supra, and I must so agree particularly where the situation arises that the mortgage is in a state where it has matured—that the time had arrived where the mortgage should have been paid off in full. There being a judgment involving the same land, the same mortgage, and the same parties, it must follow that principle of res judicata applies in the present instance and the plaintiff could not or ought not to have been able to commence this action once having obtained the judgment in the previous action. The plaintiff however, purported to discontinue the action by filing a discontinuance as above mentioned, on 7th June 1983. Would the filing of the discontinuance of action in the previous action have cured the problem of res judicata? I find that it would not, for the same reasons as stated by Funduk, Master in the Mfr. Life Ins. Co. case, supra, would apply. One cannot logically discontinue an action that has gone to judgment. Maple Credit Ltd. v. S.O.N. Holdings Ltd. (1983), 29 Alta. L.R. (2d) 162 (Q.B.), at 164-65, per Decore J. 8. A Discontinuance May Evidence a Settlement Whether the filing of a discontinuance of action evidences a settlement will depend upon the intent of the parties. In Mellon (Next Friend of) v. Gore Mutual Insurance Co. (1995), 29 Alta. L.R. (3d) 386 (Q.B.), Lefsrud J. found that the parties intended that a matter be settled when a discontinuance was filed even though a release was not obtained. At pp. 389-90, his Lordship said: On April 14, 1994, more than one year after the Discontinuance was filed but, as I am informed, within a year from the date upon which the original negligence action was finalized, the solicitors for the plaintiff filed a second Statement of Claim based on the Family Protection Endorsement. In addressing the question as to whether or not a binding settlement agreement was reached in the first Endorsement action so as to preclude the commencement of the second action, I was well aware of the fact that at the time the Discontinuance was filed, no releases were requested or signed. I was further cognizant of the fact that along the way the Defendant … forbore making the application for summary judgment and, in accepting the Discontinuance, did not request costs. In any event, I reiterate my view that, at the time that the solicitors for the plaintiff completed, filed and forwarded the Discontinuance to the solicitors [for another interested party] who in turn passed same on to the solicitors for the Defendant, it was understood and accepted by those concerned that the claim had been settled and was at an end. The signing of a release at that time would have only provided further confirmation of what had already been accomplished. The Court of Appeal [(1995)34 Alta. L.R. (3d) 125] allowed an appeal of Lefsrud J.'s order granting summary judgment. At pp. 125-26, Lieberman J.A. said: It is not manifestly clear or beyond a reasonable doubt that there is not a triable issue raised in the pleadings herein. It is apparent from the affidavits filed that there is a dispute as to whether or not a settlement, including an agreement not to commence another action following the discontinuance of the initial action, had been reached between the solicitors involved. It appears that the Court of Appeal did not disagree that the filing of a discontinuance could act as a settlement. Rather, the court was simply stating that in the facts of this case, there existed a triable issue as to settlement and that therefore the learned chambers judge should not have granted summary judgment. 9. Discontinuance of a Class Proceeding In Mewburn v. Peers, 2013 ABQB 299, 2013 CarswellAlta 829, 50 C.P.C. (7th) 197, A.C.J. Rooke discussed discontinuance of a class proceeding. At paragraphs 20–22, his Lordship said: 20 If discontinuation of the action as a class proceeding under the Act is to be considered, the question of what the appropriate terms and conditions should be, depends on the circumstances of the case. In Smith v. Crown Life Insurance Co., [2002] O.J. No. 5539, which was considered by Slatter J. at para. 6, the application was brought to discontinue a class action before certification because a settlement had been reached with the named plaintiffs. The Court required reasonable notice to be given to the class members before the discontinuance would be allowed. In Vennell v. Barnardo's (2004) 73 O.R. (3d) 13 the Court considered an application to discontinue the class proceeding and continue the action as an individual action, and leave was granted because the court was satisfied that appropriate notice had been given to the potential members of the class. In the Davey v. CNR decision itself, Slatter J. was concerned that media coverage of this proceeding being initiated as a class action, might mean that some individuals could be under the mistaken impression that the class proceeding is ongoing and that they are members of the class. To avoid that prejudice, the plaintiff had agreed to issue a notification to the broader public, even though they had not issued a press release in the first instance (para.9). See also Hudson v. Austin 2010 ONSC 2789 (Perell J.), particularly at paras. 16, 32–37 and 42-43. 21 The question arose during the application, as to whether prejudice to the Defendants was a relevant consideration. This question was considered in Campbell v. Canada (Attorney General) 2009 FC 30 at para. 10–12, where Hansen J. found that Slatter J. (in Davey v. CNR) “… was only concerned with the possible prejudice to the putative class members.” She went on to say that she was “… not persuaded that potential prejudice to the Defendants is a relevant factor on this motion.” This finding was noted in Durling v. Sunrise Propane Energy Group Inc.[2009] O.J. No. 5969 at para. 19-20, where Cullity J. stated that “Hansen J. held that prejudice to the defendants was not a relevant consideration and that, in the absence of prejudice to the class, approval to discontinue would be granted.” He went on to note that this … acceptance that potential prejudice to the class was the “central consideration” is obviously consistent with the recommendations of the Law Reform Commission and the statement of the Court of Appeal in Sollen that the requirement of court approval is intended for the protection of class members. (referring to Sollen v. Pfizer Canada Inc. 2008 ONCA 803, and to the Ontario Law Reform Commission in its Report on Class Actions, Ministry of the Attorney General, 1982). 22 I am in agreement with this view that the protections in s. 35(1) are intended for the protection of the members of the class, or potential class, not the defendants. 10. Discontinuance of a Matrimonial Property Action In Richardson v. Richardson, 2018 ABCA 327, 2018 CarswellAlta 2260, 75 Alta. L.R. (6th) 1, a husband and wife separated, and the husband filed a Statement of Claim for Divorce and Division of Matrimonial Property. In his Prayer for Relief, he claimed “an Order for the distribution of all of the property acquired by the Plaintiff and the Defendant, either jointly or separately, in such manner as the Court deems just and equitable”. The wife filed a Demand for Notice. Eventually some of the matrimonial property was sold and distributed to the parties, but $29,000 remained paid into court. Court orders were obtained requiring the husband to provide certain financial disclosure. When he failed to do so, the wife brought an application for an order finding the husband in contempt and granting her leave to file a Statement of Defence and Counterclaim. The husband sought to discontinue the action. The Court of Appeal concluded that “different considerations apply” when it is a matrimonial property action which is sought to be discontinued (paragraph 16). The Court said: 11 An ordinary statement of claim differs from one that asserts relief that is beneficial to both parties. Take, for example, a statement of claim arising from a motor vehicle accident in which both the plaintiff and the defendant were injured. If the plaintiff commences an action for damages, the defendant has a number of options. If the defendant admits liability for the accident, and admits that the plaintiff is entitled to some damages, a demand for notice would be sufficient. On the other hand, if the defendant alleges that the plaintiff was wholly or partly responsible for the accident, and the defendant also wants to make a claim for his damages, then a defence and counterclaim is essential. It is unheard of for one of the motorists to commence an action alleging that both drivers were negligent, and seeking an award of damages for both of them for their respective injuries. That, however, is the effect of the statement of claim and demand for notice in this matrimonial property action. 12 When the respondent signalled that he was prepared to abandon his claim for a matrimonial property division, the appellant responded that she was not prepared to abandon her claim. In the circumstances, her option was to file a statement of defence and counterclaim. That required the permission of the Court under R. 3.34(5). Replacing a Demand for Notice with a Statement of Defence is in some respects analogous to amending a pleading, and may implicitly involve the withdrawal of an admission. 13 Whether a defendant who has filed a demand for notice should be permitted to file a statement of defence is a discretionary matter requiring a consideration of all the circumstances surrounding the claim. In this appeal they include: (a) The fact that the original claim was for a “just and equitable” distribution which would benefit both parties, not just relief in favour of the respondent. The appellant is not seeking to withdraw any admission that would prejudice the respondent; (b) The fact that the appellant admitted that the relief requested was appropriate, and demanded notice of any applications in the proceedings. This is not, for example, a case where the defendant allowed herself to be noted in default: Coyle v. Coyle Estate, 2005 ABQB 436, 56 Alta. L.R. (4th) 373, 383 A.R. 135 (Alta. Q.B.); (c) The appellant's legitimate expectation that the matrimonial property would be divided by the Court on the basis requested by the respondent, particularly in light of the fact that the matrimonial home was sold in these proceedings, and the proceeds partly distributed; (d) Any delay in applying. There has been inordinate delay in these proceedings, and the limitation period for commencing a new matrimonial property action has expired. Some of that delay is attributable to the involvement of the Law Society, some to the failure of the respondent to disclose his assets, and some to the appellant for failing to prosecute the litigation more aggressively. However, when the respondent indicated he intended to discontinue, the appellant moved promptly; (e) The conduct of the parties. The respondent appears to have been persistently in default of his obligation to make financial disclosure. Such a litigant is not entitled to any indulgences from the Court; and (f) Any prejudice that would result to either party. Since the appellant does not intend to deny that the relief claimed by the respondent was appropriate she is not seeking to withdraw an admission, and there is no other prejudice to the respondent. This is not for example a case where one of the spouses has since died: Coyle Estate. 14 The chambers judge proceeded on the assumption that the respondent could discontinue the action as a matter of right, absent an abuse of process: R. 4.36. The reasons under appeal do not note the nature of the relief the respondent claimed in his statement of claim, nor do they consider all of the factors just listed. Even if the respondent was able to discontinue his claim as a matter of right, that did not preclude the appellant from receiving permission of the court to file a defence and counterclaim. On this record, the appellant has met the test for substituting her Demand for Notice with a Statement of Defence and Counterclaim. Discontinuing an Action 15 In an ordinary situation, R. 4.36 permits the filing of a discontinuance as of right before a trial date is set. The Court has jurisdiction to preclude the discontinuance of an action when that would amount to an abuse of process: De Shazo. Abuse of process is a flexible concept that can encompass many misuses of civil procedure: Behn v. Moulton Contracting Ltd., 2013 SCC 26 (S.C.C.) at paras. 39-40, [2013] 2 S.C.R. 227 (S.C.C.). A discontinuous could be prevented, for example where it would be “obstructive, abusive or unfair”: De Shazo at para. 13. 16 The rule permitting the filing of a discontinuance as of right assumes the ordinary situation where the plaintiff only claims relief for himself or herself. A discontinuance essentially amounts to the plaintiff abandoning the claim. A discontinuance of this matrimonial property claim, however, would not only be an abandonment by the plaintiff of his claim for a just and equitable distribution of matrimonial property. That discontinuance also undermines the appellant's admission that such a just and equitable distribution was called for. Different considerations apply. 17 Further, a discontinuance can be prevented when there are still outstanding issues between the parties. In particular, in this action there is still $29,000 in court. The order under appeal does not explain how that sum of money is to be dealt with if the action is discontinued. There was also the outstanding issue of the respondent's failure to comply with the two disclosure orders, and the application for contempt that had been brought. Discontinuing the action does not automatically “discontinue” any court orders, and it does not automatically excuse any prior contempt. 18 In this case, it was a reviewable error for the chambers judge to deal with the application to discontinue first. The proper order of proceeding was: (a) First, to deal with the application for contempt; (b) Second, to deal with the application to file a statement of defence and counterclaim; and (c) Third, to deal with the application to prevent the respondent from discontinuing the action. At that stage it was necessary to deal with the outstanding issues, namely the $29,000 still in court, and the respondent's outstanding obligation to disclose his assets. The chambers judge dealt with the discontinuance issue first, and therefore did not find it necessary to deal with the first two issues. 19 The respondent acknowledged that he has not complied with the two disclosure orders. That admission should have disentitled him to a discontinuance, and entitled the appellant to a remedy for his contempt. Further, permitting the discontinuance would result in prejudice to the appellant. If the action was discontinued before the appellant filed her counterclaim, she would lose her claim to matrimonial property. The respondent, on the other hand, can demonstrate no prejudice since he himself is the one who proposed a just and equitable distribution.
